list.listitem: Oxygenation via simple airway manouvers followed by early intubation and ventilation is imperative for coma due to traumatic brain injury. Intubation should also be considered in all other causes of coma. B

Mechanically ventilated patients should be managed using the FASTHUG protocol (Feeding, Analgesia, Sedation holidays, Thromboembolic Prophylaxis, Elevation of the head of the bed, Ulcer Prophylaxis, Glucose control) and spontaneous breathing trials. B
Targeted temperature management improves survival and reduces rates of poor neurological outcome in patients comatose after cardiac arrest. A

Death or poor neurological outcome in comatose patients after cardiac arrest may be predicted using a variety of clinical signs, two neurophysiological studies and a serum test to guide the clinician and family in decision-making regarding the continuation or withdrawal of treatment. B
Prognosis depends heavily on the underlying aetiology. B

background.definition: Coma is the absence of wakefulness and awareness. Wakefulness is the presence of sleep/wake cycles on electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, while awareness is the capacity for environmental interaction.

list.listitem: Non-traumatic coma is a clinical syndrome with a very wide range of potential underlying diagnoses. There is significant hospital disease coding overlap between 'coma' and the diseases that cause or are associated with it. The causes of coma also vary significantly geographically. As a result, reliable statistics on the incidence non-traumatic coma are not available.

Over the last 5 years, UK national statistics suggest 'neurological support' is required in between 8 to 10% of ICU patients (ICU being the primary destination for most comatose patients) many of which experience periods of coma during their stay in ICU
The average cost per patient per day in intensive care for any reason is US$4665 with a range of US$2802 to US$6529.
Comatose patients usually require multi-organ support including invasive ventilation resulting in a cost at the higher end of this range.
Ethicolegal implications of coma in the short term include setting limitations on treatments and deciding when to withdraw life support.

In the long-term, the neurological sequelae of coma raise the issues of healthcare costs and quality of life (e.g. persistent vegetative state and other forms of severe neurological disability in 5 to 25% depending on etiology).

Intensive care delirium is a multifactorial delirium often seen in critically ill patients that develops as a result of both the critical illness and the administration of necessary sedative and analgesic agents. Coma doubles the risk of intensive care delirium (51-54% vs 20% of patients, coma vs non-coma intensive care patients, respectively). Intensive care delirium is associated with both short and medium term increase in mortality (2.5 and 3.2 fold respectively) as well as duration of mechanical ventilation, length of ICU and hospital stay, with the associated burden on healthcare resources.,,, ICU delirium is also associated with long term cognitive deficits comparable to mild-moderate alzheimer's dementia.
Distinguish traumatic brain injury from non-traumatic brain injury
Traumatic brain injury

listitem.strong: Non-traumatic causes, in order of frequency

list.listitem: Poisoning: common agents are alcohol, tricyclic antidepressants, benzodiazepines, opioids, neuroleptics and acetaminophen.

Neurological disorders: cerebral hypoxia (including post-arrest hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy), raised intracranial pressure with brainshift, ischemic total anterior circulation stroke, posterior circulation strokes affecting the brainstem and acute stroke in which there is pre-existing cerebral disease; intracranial haemorrhage, brain tumour.
Metabolic: hypercapnia, severe acidosis including diabetic ketoacidosis, hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolar coma, hyperammonaemia and severe electrolyte disturbances.
Epileptogenic: status epilepticus including non-convulsive status, post-ictal states.
Infectious and/or inflammatory : meningoencephalitis (including autoimmune), severe sepsis.

Be aware that these causes may co-exist, e.g. a meningitic patient that has developed seizures and a severe metabolic acidosis with hyponatraemia. A mnemonic ("TINNED VAMP" ) can provide a methodical way to work through possible causes when treating the comatose patient (see ).

The reticular activating system (from the dorsal pons and midbrain) and its ascending neural projections to the cerebral cortices (mostly via the thalamus) are essential to the control of consciousness.
Important neurotransmitters involved in these neural pathways are acetylcholine, noradrenaline, serotonin, histamine, glutamate and dopamine.
Links between this system and the hypothalamus determine daily sleep-wake cycles.

Functional and/or structural interruption of communication within this system may result in coma. To produce coma, structural insults usually require either extensive bilateral cerebral hemispheric lesions (which may manifest as a new unilateral lesion on a background of old contralateral disease), bilateral thalamic lesions, or lesions involving of the upper brainstem affecting the midbrain or dorsolateral pons.
The Glasgow coma scale is useful for monitoring conscious level trends in both traumatic and non-traumatic coma patients. B,,,,

Where comatose states are inconsistent with the clinical context or lasting greater than 4 weeks, use the Neurobehavioral Criteria () to rule out other forms of altered consciousness or the locked-in syndrome. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Sleep-wake cycles present. Opens eyes spontaneously, moves eyes to command. Non-fluctuating, persistent condition.
Sleep-wake cycles present. Fluctuating capacity for eye opening, visual tracking and response to command. Persistent condition.
Sleep-wake cycles present. Capacity for eye opening and visual tracking but no movements to command. Non-fluctuating, persistent condition.
Sleep-wake cycles present. Capacity for eye opening but no visual tracking or movement to command. Non-fluctuating, persistent condition.
Transient condition with fluctuating conscious level and attention.

list.listitem: Simply, coma is 'unfluctuating eyes-closed unconsciousness'. The exception to this is the presence of ptosis in other states of altered consciousness and the locked-in syndrome. The "locked-in syndrome" is classically described in relation to discrete lesions of the ventral or rostral pons but may be reproduced by profound widespread distal lesions such as Guillain-barre, botulism, myasthenic crises, organophosphate poisoning, and envenomation by snakes and other animals with specific neurotoxins. Thus, visual tracking should be routinely tested repeatedly in all patients with eyes held open where necessary and an awareness of these differentials used to trigger further investigation when neuroimaging does not demonstrate a cause and other common causes have been ruled out . See Table above for differential diagnoses of coma. In coma, both sleep-wake cycles and awareness are absent. Several days of repeated neurological examination may be necessary to establish true coma and unless brainstem death is suspected and confirmed, at least 72 hours or more of observation is frequently required before prognostication is possible.

The Glasgow Coma Scale can be used reliably to assess conscious level trends in patients with both traumatic and non-traumatic coma. In particular, a fall in Glasgow coma scale correlates with deteriorations in CT findings and the need for intervention in both adults and children who have sustained traumatic brain injuries.

For the definitive diagnosis of coma, use the Neurobehavioral Criteria (). These criteria differentiate between coma and other forms of altered consciousness which form the differential diagnoses for coma.

Where comatose states (as idenitified by Glasgow Coma Scale less than 9) are out of keeping with the clinical context or lasting greater than 4 weeks, seek an alternative diagnoses and use the Neurobehavioral Criteria () to help rule out other forms of altered consciousness or the locked-in syndrome.

Following CT imaging, where intracranial infection is suspected, prompt lumbar puncture should be performed in the absence of contraindication (local sepsis, evidence of transtentorial/tranforaminal pressure gradients on CT, coagulopathy, cardiorespiratory instability). CSF bacterial sterilisation is complete 8 hours after IV antibacterials in the majority of cases, and viral PCR and bacterial PCR becomes unreliable 48 hours and 96 hours respectively after antimicrobials are given. Unnecessary delays to lumbar puncture confuses diagnosis and the determination of appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

Low grades of evidence exist for the use of intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring in traumatic brain injury. Only one RCT exists and did not demonstrate superiority over clinical examination and imaging in traumatic brain injury. A systematic review of largely observational studies also found overall no impact on mortality of using ICP, but if limited to 7 cohort studies since 2012 there was a reduction in mortality (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.78). However, ICP monitoring was also associated with longer length of stay. ICP monitoring is not recommended in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage or cerebral/cerebellar infarct with swelling.
For the diagnosis of brain death, see UK and US diagnostic criteria for clinical diagnosis of brain death and brain stem death in adults in and .

Even if ventilation and cardiovascular support are continued, both adults and children will ultimately suffer cessation of heartbeat in the presence of brainstem death (usually within a few days but occasionally weeks to months if aggressive support is used).

Bilaterally absent median nerve somatosensory evoked potentials (in the absence of artifact during the test) 72 hours or more after the onset of persisting hypoxic-ischemia coma (with GCS motor score 1-2) are strongly predictive of death or persistent vegetative state (positive predictive value = 100% in an existing meta-analysis and false positive rate 0% in an RCT) and remain as reliable under therapeutic hypothermia. Median nerve evoked potentials are known to be more reliable in the presence of metabolic derangements and drugs as compared with other prognostic parameters but should be interpreted with caution especially where such conditions are reversible.

A systematic review identified 41 studies of somatosensory evoked potentials (SEP) to predict the likelihood of awakening in different kinds of coma:
Adult hypoxic/ischemic encephalopathy: SEP absent: 0% (95% CI 0-1), abnormal: 22% (17%-26%), normal: 52% (48%-56%) Adult intracranial hemorrhage: SEP absent: 1% (0%-4%); present: 38% (27%-48%) Adult or adolescent traumatic brain injury: SEP absent: 5% (2%-7%); abnormal: 70% (64%-75%); normal: 89% (85%-92%) Child or teen: SEP absent: 7% (4%-10%); abnormal: 69% (61%-77%); normal 86% (80%-92%)

EEG burst suppression pattern, status epilepticus, or isoelectric 72 hours or more after onset of persistent hypoxic-ischemic coma in adults strongly predicts death or persistent vegetative state. EEG is not as reliable as evoked potentials, particularly in the presence of sedative drugs or hypothermia, but may be useful in the absence of these when used in combination with at least one of several other negatively prognostic features (e.g. high neurone specific enolase, clinical myoclonic status, and diffuse anoxic injury on CT/MRI) in patients who are comatose at 72 hours in deciding on the withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. Absence of EEG reactivity has also been shown to strongly correlate with poor outcome but is associated with greater interrater variability in terms of method of stimulation and end points in reactivity.

The presence of evoked potentials are poor at predicting good outcome; they are useful solely as predictors of poor outcome when they are absent. Thus, bilaterally absent potentials can help guide decisions around withdrawing life support in comatose patients after cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and provide prognostic information for families.

High neurone specific enolase (NSE) levels measured at 24, 48 and 72 hours demonstrating a consistent upward trend alongside an absolute level at 72 hours > 50 ng/ml reliably predicts poor outcome in patients with persisting coma at 72 hours post arrest, regardless of temperature targeted. Owing to variations in the way NSE is measured and levels reported, it should be used only in combination with other markers of poor outcome as described above. Care should be taken with units of measure used by any given lab.

A Glasgow coma scale <= 8 approximates the Neurobehavioural Criteria () for day to day use. The {Glasgow coma scale | Rule 114} does not reliably distinguish between coma and the differential diagnoses of apparent coma. However, decreases in the Glasgow coma scale correlate well with deteriorations in intracranial pathology in moderate and severe head injury. It is also useful {for prognosis | HP 128}.
A validated clinical decision rule can help estimate the prognosis of patients with nontraumatic coma.
For the initial management of coma, see .
Intubation and ventilation when GCS< or =8 for traumatic coma reduces mortality from 45% to 32% and increases proportions making full recovery or with moderate disability from 40% to 58%.

Mechanically ventilated patients should be managed using the FASTHUG protocol (Feeding, Analgesia, Sedation holidays, Thromboembolic Prophylaxis, Elevation of the head of the bed, Ulcer Prophylaxis, Glucose control) and spontaneous breathing trials.

There is no strong evidence to advocate or refute intubation and ventilation in non-traumatic coma. The risks of intubation and ventilation should be weighed against the perceived risks of a conservative approach (regular monitoring, supplemental oxygen and airway adjuncts). Some non-traumatic comatose states may be rapidly reversed with appropriate treatment, negating the need for intubation.
In hypoglycaemic patients, who are thiamine deficient, administration of dextrose containing fluids without concomitant thiamine replacement may precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.
For the management of coma beyond the initial stages, see .

Coma rarely persists longer than 4 weeks: confirmation of coma using neurobehavioural criteria must be attained and alternative diagnoses of altered consciousness must be sought (see Differential Diagnosis)

Delirium is a transient state of fluctuating reduced conscious level and attention deificits. It occurs in 51-54% of patients recovering from coma. The well validated CAM-ICU assessment can be used to screen for and monitor this condition in ventilated patients.
For coma due to traumatic brain injury, early intubation and ventilation improve outcomes. B
Consider hemodialysis for selected patients with poisoning with salicylate, phenobarbital, lithium, ethylene glycol and valproate and with isolated hyperammonaemia. C
Consider urinary alkalinisation in salicylate and tricyclic overdose. C

In patients comatose after surviving cardiac arrest, use targeted temperature management to acheive a target temperature within 8 hours of return of spontaneous circulation, and continue for 24 hours. A

In intubated patients, the FASTHUG ventilator care bundle (Feeding, Analgesia, Sedation holidays, Thromboembolic Prophylaxis, Elevation of the head of the bed, Ulcer Prophylaxis, Glucose control), daily spontaneous breathing trials and sedation holidays are recommended. B

Flumazenil may be given 10 mcg/kg (pediatric) or in 100 mcg increments up to 1mg (adults) in benzodiazepine overdose. it should used with caution in patients at risk of seizures (including chronic alcohol abuse, chronic benzodiazepine use and tricyclic antidepressant overdose). it has a shorter half life than many benzodiazepines: patients should therefore be monitored for resedation and given supplemental oxygen.

Naloxone is safe for reversal of opiate overdose. Give 10 mcg/kg in children or 400 mcg increments up to 10 mg in adults. It also has a shorter half life than many opiates. Thus, following recovery, patients should be monitored for resedation and respiratory depression and given supplemental oxygen.

IV sodium bicarbonate should be considered in salicylate overdose when arterial blood pH <7.3 with the aim to correct to pH 7.4. Urinary alkalinisation using IV bicarbonate is recommended when plasma salicylate is 600-800 mg/L in adults or 450-700 mg/L in children and the elderly. Hourly urine pH should be measured and maintained at pH 7.5-8.5. Plasma electrolytes should be measured every 3 hours. Forced diuresis is not recommended because it provides little benefit whilst causing a number of potentially serious side effects. Also consider urinary alkalinisation in patients with tricyclic antidepressant overdose with cardiovascular toxicity.
Chelating agents should be used in heavy metal poisoning.

Treatment in overdose of phenothiazines, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, amphetamines and ecstasy is supportive. Cyproheptadine, a selective serotonin antagonist, may be used where drugs with known serotonergic components produce refractory serotonergic features but should be guided where possible by specialist poisoning or toxicology services.
The management of cocaine toxicity is supportive with specific measures for cardiovascular sequelae (hypertensive crises, acute coronary syndromes and arrythmias).

The evidence based management of intracranial vascular events (subarachnoid haemorrhage, acute stroke, intracranial haematomas, intracerebral haemorrhage), traumatic brain injury, intracranial infection (encephalitis, meningitis, brain abscess), hypoglycaemia and diabetic emergencies are outlined in their respective chapters.
There is no reliable evidence to support or refute the use of sensory stimulation in comatose patients (traumatic or non-traumatic) to speed recovery or alter outcome.

Carbon monoxide poisoning is managed with oxygen therapy, the form of which depends on the clinical situation. There is no definitive evidence for the duration of oxygen therapy but repeated blood carboxyhemoglobin measurements should be considered in severe poisoning to rule out secondary peaks in carboxyhemoglobin levels 24 to 36 hours after the acute exposure due to cytochrome washout.

In-hospital target temperature management (32-36C for 24 hours), with a target temperature achieved within 8 hours of return of spontaneous circulation, is recommended for patients who have GCS <8 following return of spontaneous circulation after cardiac arrest to improve survival. Patients presenting with non-shockable rhythms may benefit (in terms of neurological outcome) from the lower end of this temperature range, while shockable rhythms can be targeted to 36C to 37.5C., Cooling should be performed using either systems with automated continuous thermastatic control. Rewarming should be active and controlled at 0.25 to 0.5 degrees centigrade per hour to avoid hypotension and rebound hyperthermia. The complications of hypothermia include arrhythmias and coagulopathy and may indicate the need to discontinue the therapy. Hypothermia should not be used in cases of severe cardiogenic shock.

A clinical trial randomized 119 patients with severe traumatic brain injury to intracranial pressure (ICP) plus brain tissue oxygenation monitoring versus ICP monitoring alone. Patients receiving both forms of monitoring had a smaller proportion of time with brain tissue hypoxia, and a trend toward reduced mortality.
For comatose patients in acute or acute-on-chronic liver failure, there in insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of artifical liver support systems.

Use of the FASTHUG ventilator care bundle (daily evaluation of Feeding, Analgesia, Sedation holidays, Thromboembolic Prophylaxis, Elevation of the head of the bed, Ulcer Prophylaxis, Glucose control) reduces incidence of ventilator associated pneumonia in ventilated patients from 19.3/1000 to 7.3/1000 ventilator-days. Other modifications and developments of this bundle have since suggested an association between methodical, bundled ICU care and lower short term mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, incidence of coma and delirium, intensive care readmission, and dependent living after discharge.

Use of daily sedation holidays of at least 4 hours and spontaneous breathing trials in mechanically ventilated patients significantly reduce length of stay in ICU, in the hospital, and mortality rates.
A 'Wake up and Breathe' flowchart is available.
A Cochrane review concluded that there is no clear guidance regarding the efficacy of therapeutic position using head of bed elevation.

Based on limited quality and quantity of data, a systematic review of eight studies concluded that early tracheotomy (<10 days after injury) with the primary intention of weaning from sedation and mechanical ventilation in patients with severe traumatic brain injury is associated with shorter ICU length of stay, shorter duration of mechanical ventilation, and a lower incidence of pneumonia. This may not be reproducible in other critically ill patient groups and tracheostomy for this purpose within 4 days of commencement of mechanical ventilation is generally not recommended.
Renal replacement therapy (RRT) is indicated in comatose patients in the following situations:

Salicylate overdose: haemodialysis reduces morbidity and mortality in severe metabolic acidosis pH <7.2, pulmonary oedema, acute renal failure and when plasma salicylate levels are >800mg/L (adults) or >700mg/L (children and elderly).
Phenobarbital overdose: consider hemodialysis in the presence of severe hypotension or prolonged coma.

Lithium overdose: consider hemodialysis in patients with neurological toxicity (coma, confusion, or seizures). Sub-acutely developing toxicity may be possible at lower serum lithium levels than acute toxicity due to tissue/intracellular sequestration Monitor plasma lithium levels 6 to 8 hours after dialysis to detect rebound rises in lithium levels as a result of redistribution.
Ethylene glycol toxicity: in the presence of severe metabolic acidosis, acute renal failure, pulmonary or cerebral oedema and when plasma levels >0.5g/L, hemodialysis is indicated.
Valproate overdose: hemodialysis is indicated in the presence of severe hypotension, coma, hyperammonaemia, severe metabolic acidosis or when plasma levels >850mg/L.

Isolated Hyperammonaemia: given its rare incidence out of the context of acute liver failure, evidence-based guidance on the use of RRT is limited however it should be considered in patients with encephalopathy or with levels 3 times the upper limit of normal where the underlying pathology is felt to be reversible. In the context of liver failure, the value of RRT remains uncertain unless used as part of a bridge to transplantation and when used for acute renal failure, is associated with a high mortality.
For acute hepatic encephalopathy, enteral lactulose should be started with a low threshold for the addition of enteral rifaximin.

Delirium is very common in patients emerging from coma. It is associated with significantly increased mortality and hospital cost, and is the one of strongest predictors of prolonged ICU and hospital stay. The CAM-ICU assessment tool may be used to identify and monitor this complication.
At least one third of patients surviving critical illness will experience long-term cognitive impairment consistent with mild to moderate dementia.

A best practices management protocol for ICU delirium is available. This focuses on encouraging patients to come off sedation, breath for themselves and orientate as soon as is possible. It also encourages clinicians to rule out organic causes and withdraw possible culprit drugs that may be contributing and introduce appropriate medication where necessary to control pain and agitation.

Ventilator-associated pneumonia is a significant risk in comatose patients who require mechanical ventilation and is associated with significant mortality (up to 50%), cost ($5000-$20000 per diagnosis) and an increase in length of hospital stay (from 4-13 days).
Prognosis depends heavily on the underlying aetiology. B

For patients comatose after cardiac arrest, poor neurological outcome or death at discharge and up to 12 months later may be predicted using a series of clinical signs at 72 hours postarrest (GCS Motor score 1-2 with both bilaterally absent pupillary light and corneal reflexes) and by neurophysiological testing (EEG, bilateral median nerve somatosensory evoked potentials and neurone specific enolase). The European Resuscitation Council and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine have published a useful prognostication algorithm to guide clinicians. B

A systematic review of 94 studies with 30,200 experiencing coma after cardiac arrest concluded that bilaterally absent pupillary or corneal reflex after day 4, elevated neuron-specific enolase at 24 hours, absent N20 waves or short-latency somatosensory-evoked potentials, seizures on EEG, diffuse cerebral edema on brain CT after 2 hours, or reduced diffusion on brain MRI after 2 to 5 dayspredict poor outcome.
Coma rarely persists beyond 4eks: the diagnosis of alternative states of consciousness should be sought. Neurobehavioral Criteria () are available for the identification of these states. C
The natural history varies markedly with the aetiology. Coma may be regarded as the transitional state from initial insult to full or incomplete neurological recovery, or brain death.
Transition from coma towards full or incomplete brain recovery is marked by the return of sleep wake cycles.

Comatose states rarely continue beyond 4 weeks from initial insult. Either recovery ensues, brain death has occurred or patients reach various possible states of persistent chronically depressed consciousness, evident with the return of sleep wake cycles but impaired awareness.

In the presence of brainstem death, body organs undergo necrosis and fail, ultimately resulting in cardiac arrest within days as a result of a lack of central integration of their functions. This occurs even despite aggressive cardiorespiratory support, although the time delay to arrest may be prolonged by up to several weeks. There are no reports of recovery of brainstem function during this interval.
Stroke and post-cardiac arrest coma carries a particularly poor prognosis.

The American Academy of Neurology, European Resuscitation Council and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine have published graded evidence-based guidance on the use of history, clinical signs, biochemistry, neurophysiological testing and neuroimaging in predicting outcome after cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

The likelihood of poor neurological outcome or death in adults (by discharge, 6 months or 12 months) may be guided using clinical signs at 24, 48 and 72 hours. Poor neurological outcome is defined as Cerebral Performance Category 3-5 (see ).

A systematic review of 94 studies with 30,200 experiencing coma after cardiac arrest concluded that bilaterally absent pupillary or corneal reflex after day 4, elevated neuron-specific enolase at 24 hours, absent N20 waves or short-latency somatosensory-evoked potentials, seizures on EEG, diffuse cerebral edema on brain CT after 2 hours, or reduced diffusion on brain MRI after 2 to 5 dayspredict poor outcome.

EEG, bilateral median nerve somatosensory evoked potentials at 72 hours or more and serial serum neurone specific enolase at 24, 48 and 72 hours after onset of hypoxic-ischemic coma in adults can be used to predict poor outcome (death or persistent vegetative state).
The role of neurophysiology in other causes of non-traumatic coma is not well established.
Data describing the prognosis of other causes of non-traumatic coma and patients with persistent altered states of consciousness is dated (older than 10 years). More up to date research is required.
Previous traumatic brain injury including coma is associated with an increase in the likelihood of all-cause and vascular dementia but not Alzheimer's dementia.
The following may cause coma from as early as 20 weeks gestation up to the early post -partum period.
Pre-eclampsia leading to hypertensive crises and coagulopathy predispose to intracranial haemorrhage.
Eclampsia.
Hepatic failure resulting from HELLP syndrome.
In the post-partum period following major obstetric haemorrhage, anterior pituitary failure (Sheehan's syndrome) should be considered.
The aetiology of non-traumatic coma differs from the adult population.

The most common causes, in order of frequency, are: sepsis (mainly systemic, intracranial and respiratory sepsis), poisoning, epileptogenic, complications of congenital abnormalities (mainly congenital heart disease and hydrocephalus), accidents (asphyxia and burns), metabolic imbalance, spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage, asthma and complications of malignancy.

Various pediatric adaptations of the Glasgow coma scale have been attempted. Only one (see ) has high sensitivity and specificity for abnormal CT findings requiring intervention in children with blunt head trauma. The adult Glasgow coma scale can be used reliably in children older than 2 years.

In the UK, for children older than 2 months, the adult method for diagnosis of brain death may be used. In children less than 2 months old, it is viewed as rarely possible to reliably diagnose brainstem death.

In the US, guidelines exist for term neonates up to 18 years of age. These criteria differ from the UK in terms of specifying specific time intervals between the two brainstem testing observations and in its support in the use ancillary tests where there are problems with clinical testing.

The diagnosis of altered states of consciousness (e.g. persistent vegetative state) is difficult before 3 months of age because many higher cognitive functions, such as voluntary responses, are undeveloped.
The role of neurophysiology in prognostication in adults is not transferable to the pediatric population. Results from these tests are confounded by variable levels of brain maturity.

feature.caption: Causes of coma using the mnemonic “TINNED VAMP”.
feature.feature_body:
Trauma, Toxins
Trauma: Traumatic Brain Injury (cerebral contusions, diffuse axonal injury) Intracerebral, Subarachnoid, Subdural or Extradural Haemorrhage
Toxins: Drugs- overdose and idiosyncratic reactions (Serotonin Syndrome, Malignant Neuroleptic Syndrome) Carbon Monoxide Heavy Metals
Inflammatory- infectious and non infectious Infectious: Meningitis Encephalitis Cerebral Abscess
Non-infectious: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (may also be secondary to infection) Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis and other forms of post- and para-infectious, paraneoplastic and autoimmune encephalitis
Neoplastic
Brain Tumour (including associated haemorrhage or oedema)
Nutritional
Wernicke's Encephalopathy
Endocrine
Panhypopituitarism Adrenal Crisis Mxyoedema Coma Thyrotoxic Storm
Developmental, Degenerative
Epilepsy (post-ictal states, convulsive and non-convulsive status)
Hydrocephalus
In-born error of metabolism/ mitochondrial disease
Vascular
Thromboembolic Stroke Cerebral Venous Thrombosis (venous sinus or cortical vein) Spontaneous Subarachnoid Haemorrhage Hypertensive Encephalopathy
Autoimmune
Cerebral Vasculitis
Metabolic
Hypoxia/Anoxia (inc cardiopulmonary arrest: ‘hypoxic-ischemic’ ) Hypercapnia Hypothermia Hypo/Hyperglycaemia Hypo/Hypernatraemia (including central pontine demyelinolysis) Hypo/Hypercalcaemia Hepatic/Hyperammonaemic Encephalopathy Uraemic Encephalopathy Reye's syndrome
Psychogenic
Psychogenic coma (dissociative disorders)
Reference: Stevens RD, Bhardwaj A. Approach to the Comatose Patient. 2006; 34; 31-41.

feature.caption: The neurobehavioural criteria. All of these features must be present for the diagnosis of coma.

tr.td: •the patient's eyes do not open either spontaneously or to external stimulations
•the patient does not follow any commands
•the patient does not mouth or utter recognizable words
•the patient does not demonstrate intentional movement (may show reflexive movement such as posturing, withdrawal from pain or involuntary smiling)
•the patients cannot sustain visual pursuit movements of the eyes through a 45 degree arc in any direction when the eyes are held open manually
•the above features are not secondary to the use of paralytic agents

feature.caption: UK Diagnostic criteria for clinical diagnosis of brain and brain stem death in adults.
feature.feature_body:
Aetiology: The patient's condition must be due to irreversible brain damage of known aetiology, which should be known to be associated with brain stem death.
Prerequisites to testing: Core temp ≥34°C No drug intoxication or poisoning Absence of sedative and neuromuscular blocking drugs No neurological disorders associated with profound neuromuscular weakness and impaired brain stem reflexes No severe endocrine disturbance Normotension: MAP >60mmHg Blood gas parameters: PaCO2 <6.0kPa PaO2 >10kPa pH 7.35 – 7.45 No electrolyte abnormalities: 115mmol/L≤Na≤160mmol/L 2mmol/L≤K 0.5mmol/L≤Mg/PO4≤3.0mmol/L 3mmol/L≤glucose≤20mmol/L
Personnel: Two medical practitioners more than 5 years registered and familiar with the tests, one of whom must be a consultant Neither should have a conflict of interest or be a member of the transplant team They should perform two sets of tests together and there is no specified time interval between the first and second tests.
Cardinal features: Coma Absence of brainstem reflexes Apnoea
Coma: Deep coma, unresponsive, artificially ventilated
Absence of brain stem reflexes: Loss of direct and consensual pupillary light reflexes Loss of corneal reflex Loss of oculovestibular reflex Loss of gag reflex Loss of cough reflex No motor response within cranial nerve distribution to supraorbital ridge pressure or to painful stimulus applied in any somatic area
Apnoea test: Preparation – increase FiO2 to 1.0 and reduce minute ventilation to allow rise in CO2. Obtain arterial blood gas sample to ensure paCO2 at least 6.0kPa and pH <7.4 (for chronic CO2 retention aim for paCO2 rise associated with pH <7.4). Disconnect from ventilator but maintain oxygenation using 5 l/min oxygen through catheter passed via endotracheal tube (apnoeic oxygenation). Observe for signs of respiratory effort for 5 minutes Repeat ABG to ensure paCO2 rise >o.5kPa from starting level Recommence ventilation with settings to allow gradual correction to pre-testing blood gas values
Additional information: If there is no evidence of brain stem function the legal time of death is when the first set of tests confirms brain stem death.
Adapted from: Academy of Royal Medical Colleges, 2008. A Code of Practice for the Diagnosis and Confirmation of Death. www.aomrc.org.uk/aomrc/admin/reports/docs/DofD-final.pdf

feature.caption: US Diagnostic criteria for clinical diagnosis of brain and brain stem death in adults.
feature.feature_body:
Etiology: Clinical or neuroimaging evidence of an acute CNS catastrophe that is compatible with the diagnosis of brain death
Prerequisites to testing: Exclusion of complicating medical condition that may affect assessment including severe electrolyte, endocrine or acid-base disturbance No drug intoxication or poisoning Core temp ≥32°C
Personnel: No specific medical practitioner specified No mandatory second test Arbitrary time interval of 6 hours recommended if second tests being undertaken
Cardinal features: Coma Absence of brainstem reflexes Apnoea
Coma/Unresponsiveness: No cerebral motor response to pain in all extremities
Absence of brain stem reflexes: Pupils in midposition and between size 4mm to 9mm Loss of pupillary light reflex Loss of oculocephalic reflex (not performed when C-spine fracture or instability is apparent) Loss of corneal reflex Loss of oculovestibular reflex No jaw reflex Loss of gag reflex Loss of cough reflex No facial grimacing to deep pressure on nail bed, supraorbital ridge or temporomandibular joint
Apnea test: Preparation – core temp ≥36.5°C, systolic BP >90mmHg, euvolaemia or positive fluid balance in previous 6 hours, paCO2 normal or ≥5.3kPa / 40mmHg, paO2 normal. Similar method for apnoeic oxygenation. Observe for signs of respiratory effort for 8 minutes Repeat ABG to ensure paCO2 ≥7.9kPa / 60mmHg or 20mmHg increase over baseline normal paCO2 Recommence ventilation at end of test or sooner if desaturation or haemodynamic instability
Additional information: In the following conditions confirmatory tests may be required to confirm brain death. Conditions: severe facial trauma, pre-existing papillary abnormalities, toxic levels of drugs including sedatives, sleep apnoea or severe pulmonary disease. Confirmatory tests: conventional cerebral angiography, EEG, transcranial Doppler ultrasonography, technetium-99m brain scan, somatosensory evoked potentials
Adapted from: Practice Parameters: Determining Brain Death in Adults. Report of the Quality Standards Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology. www.aan.com/professionals/practice/guidelines/pda/Brain_death_adults.pdf

feature.caption: Glasgow-Pittsburgh Cerebral Performance Category.
feature.feature_body:
Glasgow-Pittsburgh Cerebral Perfomance Category (CPC) Description
1.Good Cerebral Performance
Conscious: Alert, able to work and lead a normal life. May have minor psychological or neurological deficits (mild dysphasia, nonincapacitating hemiparesis, or minor cranial nerve abnormalities).
2. Moderate Cerebral Disability
Conscious. Sufficient cerebral function for part-time work in sheltered environment or independent activities of daily life (dressing, traveling by public transportation, and preparing food). May have hemiplegia, seizures, ataxia, dsysarthria, dysphasia, or permanent memory or mental changes.
3. Severe Cerebral Disability
Conscious. Dependent on others for daily support because of impaired brain function (in an institution or at home with exceptional family effort). At least limited cognition. Includes a wide range of cerebral abnormalities from ambulatory with severe memory disturbance or dementia precluding independent existence to paralytic and able to communicate only with eyes, as in the locked-in syndrome.
4. Coma, Vegetative State
Not conscious. Unaware of surroundings, no cognition. No verbal or psychological interactions with environment.
5. Death
Certified brain dead or dead by traditional criteria.
Reference: Booth CM, Boone RH,Tomlinson G, Detsky AS. Is This Patient Dead, Vegetative, or Severely Neurologically Impaired?: Assessing Outcome for Comatose Survivors of Cardiac Arrest.. 2004; 291(7): 870-879
